- HR Spotlight


# HR Spotlight: Elizabeth Odetokun on Taking Charge of Your Career


- Great G. Ufford


- November 14, 2026


Table of Contents


Toggle


Elizabeth Odetokun once had to fight for a seat at a meeting she knew she belonged in. She was the HR Manager at Mainstack. The company’s leaders made decisions without her but when problems surfaced, they expected her to solve them. So she went to the founders and asked why HR wasn’t part of those conversations.


It takes courage to fight for something you believe you should already have. She eventually got her seat at the table but she made it clear that the experience wasn’t pleasant.


Staying quiet would cost her the opportunity to learn and do more. She would also miss the chance to work closely with the company’s leaders. For her, that was too much to give up.


“Your number one responsibility is your career,” she said during the interview.


That belief has shaped how Elizabeth handles work. Six years ago, Elizabeth was an HR intern learning payroll through Google. Today, she works with founders on HR, strategy and business operations.


None of it would have happened if she waited for someone to recognise her potential.


##


How do you build a career in something you never planned for?


Elizabeth initially wanted to study Economics at Obafemi Awolowo University. She wanted to attend the school so badly that she still laughs about it today.


“For the life of me, I can’t even remember why I wanted to go to that school.” she said.


She didn’t pass the post-UTME but got into Lagos State University and chose not to attend. The school was far from home, and she had concerns about safety.


Then a family friend suggested the University of Lagos. He also advised her to consider Human Resources, a course she knew almost nothing about. His selling point was simple; with HR, she could work in almost any industry.


That sounded good enough to Elizabeth, so she went on to study HR at the University of Lagos. But it took her first internship in 2019 to find out what working in HR really meant.


On her first day, she had to screen 30 to 40 job applicants, with no prior experience. Soon, she was managing over 100 workers at the APM Terminal in Apapa. She handled recruitment, medical checks, onboarding and payroll.


Remember, this was an intern who just left school.


“I didn’t feel like an intern at all,” she recalled.


She had never prepared payroll before, let alone for 100 people. There was no detailed training to fall back on. So she turned to Google to learn how to draft memos, prepare payroll and complete other tasks.


She often worked late because she was afraid of making mistakes.


The working conditions weren’t great either. The company even cut her pay when she refused to work on some weekends. She could have left, other interns did but Elizabeth had made a deal with herself. She would spend six months there, give the job her best and leave with experience she needed.


That experience taught Elizabeth a lesson she still lives by. She couldn’t control everything at work, but she could choose how to respond.


As her career grew, she took that lesson with her. It helped her take on bigger roles, even when she lacked all the answers.


##


What happens when your role outgrows your experience?


At Bundle Africa, Elizabeth started out handling recruitment, employee engagement and performance reviews. Then the company restructured, and her senior manager left. Elizabeth began reporting directly to the Chief Operating Officer.


Suddenly, her responsibilities went far beyond managing people. She had to review departmental budgets, check invoices and question spending. She also checked how the customer service team spoke to customers. If something wasn’t right, she asked them to fix it.


It was unfamiliar work, but she didn’t shy away from it. She recalls asking department heads to explain expenses worth thousands of dollars.


“What’s going on here? What are we hoping to get here?”


She laughed as she told me how much she enjoyed having the authority to ask those questions.


“I had power, so I enjoyed having that power.”


But with that authority came more responsibility.


She had to understand the numbers, pay attention to details and defend her decisions. She couldn’t approve something simply because a department head had submitted it.


The finance team began to notice her work. One colleague was so impressed by her attention to detail that they asked if she had done the work before.


She hadn’t. She was learning every day and she wanted to do the work well.


That period changed how Elizabeth saw her place in a business. She began to see how each part of the business worked and how the decisions made in one team affected the others.


She also realised that she could contribute to conversations beyond HR.


##


What if nobody makes room for you at the table?


When Elizabeth joined Mainstack, she brought that confidence with her. But she faced a new problem. She wasn’t present in leadership meetings.


She had worked across different areas of business operations. She understood why HR needed to know what was happening across the company. Yet she still had to make her case.


Companies often involve HR in hiring and staff matters. But HR rarely gets a seat at the table when leaders make business decisions.


Elizabeth admits that some HR professionals also stick to these duties, but she wanted to do more. She had shown this curiosity before.


At Sygnite, a renewable energy company, she wanted to understand more than HR. She learnt about suppliers, equipment costs, profit margins and what the engineers did. She wasn’t trying to become an engineer. She wanted to understand what they do so she could make better decisions about the people on those teams.


At Mainstack, she put that curiosity to work by pushing for a place in leadership meetings. It wasn’t easy, and she didn’t enjoy having to fight for her place. But the decision changed her experience at the company.


She built closer relationships with the founders. They trusted her with more information and asked for her advice. Other team leads also began to turn to her for input.


A year after, she secured a 40% salary increase.


##


What has Elizabeth done everything she has learnt?


Elizabeth holds two beliefs that may seem at odds. Elizabeth believes you should know when to leave a job. But while you’re there, take every chance to learn and grow. Don’t wait for someone to give you permission.


At Zap Africa, she noticed that many first-time managers struggled to lead their teams. Many had earned promotions because they were good at their jobs. But being good at your job doesn’t automatically teach you how to manage other people.


They struggled with feedback, onboarding and performance conversations. When those problems came up, they often turned to HR. Elizabeth decided to give them a better starting point, so she created a guide in Notion.


It explained what managers needed to do and how to handle problems at work. The goal was to help them become more confident in their roles instead of waiting for HR to solve every problem.


She has also created guides to help people plan their careers and ask for better pay. One of them guides employees how to make a case for a 40% raise.


She understands that pay discussions can be difficult. A company may have limited funds, while an employee may have strong reasons for asking for more.


Her advice is to understand both sides.


Employees need to understand how companies decide what to pay. They should also be ready to show why they deserve more. But they should also know when the opportunities they want may no longer exist where they work.


That interest in people’s career choices has led Elizabeth into research. She’s now studying what makes Nigerian professionals stay in a job or choose a new one.


Career growth? Healthcare? Pension benefits? The distance to work? Or simply knowing their pay will arrive on time?


Elizabeth wants to help employers better understand what their employees value. She plans to publish her findings as a white paper to help companies attract and keep good employees. It’s quite a journey from the young intern who had to Google her way through HR tasks.


She’s now creating some of the resources she wishes more people had access to.


##


But who is Elizabeth when nobody needs anything from HR?


After years of focusing on her career, Elizabeth is making more time for life outside work.


She now makes time for her family, tries new things and enjoys life outside work. These days, she makes plans to spend time with her siblings. She creates dates for them to meet, catch up and have fun. She also has plenty of ideas she wants to try.


She started Gauge, a service that helps people prepare for important job interviews. She enjoys planning events and bringing people together. And sometimes, she wants to do things for the fun of it.
